title: Gateway calls time out instantly after the config refactor
ticket: Since this morning's config refactor every charge fails with 'context deadline exceeded', even though the payment gateway is healthy and TIMEOUT_SECONDS is still 3.

lines: func (c *Client) Charge(ctx context.Context, req ChargeRequest) (*Charge, error) {
httpReq, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, c.baseURL+"/v1/charges", bytes.NewReader(body))

output: client_test.go:41: Charge() error = Post "http://127.0.0.1:51734/v1/charges": context deadline exceeded
client_test.go:42: deadline was 3ns after the call; want 3s

explanation.cause: time.Duration(3) is three nanoseconds: a Duration counts nanoseconds, so a plain number needs a unit.
explanation.why: Every charge's context expired before the request left the process. Multiplying by time.Second restores the 3 s budget; dropping the timeout entirely would let a slow gateway pin connections forever.

title: Checkout pods hang when the fraud service stalls
ticket: During the fraud-check vendor's incident, checkout-api pods stopped answering entirely. Goroutine dumps show hundreds of requests stuck in fraudClient.Score for over ten minutes.

lines: func (c *Client) Score(ctx context.Context, order Order) (float64, error) {

output: client_test.go:77: test timed out: Score() still blocked after 30s

explanation.cause: A zero-value http.Client has no timeout, so a vendor that accepts the connection and never answers holds the request forever.
explanation.why: Each stuck call held a goroutine and a slot until the pods stopped serving anything. A client-wide Timeout bounds every call; http.DefaultClient has the same missing timeout, and Timeout: 2 would be two nanoseconds.

title: Scale checkout-api for the autumn sale
author: Sam Tan
description: Marketing expects 3x traffic on Saturday. Doubling replicas and giving each pod a bigger Hikari pool so we don't run out of connections like last time. orders-db is max_connections = 100.

explanation.cause: 6 replicas x 50 connections is 300 against a database that allows 100.
explanation.why: The first pods to start would take every slot and the rest would crash-loop on 'too many clients'. Pool size times replicas has to fit under max_connections with headroom; more replicas with the same or a smaller pool is the safe change.

title: Add a readiness probe to the order-status worker
author: Priya Nair
description: The worker gets traffic before its consumers are connected, so the first requests after every deploy 503. This adds a readiness probe on the endpoint that only returns 200 once the consumers are up.

explanation.cause: Nothing wrong: the probe checks an endpoint that reflects real readiness, with sane timings.
explanation.why: A readiness probe only takes a pod out of the load balancer, it never restarts it, so a strict check is safe here. The trap to avoid would be pointing a liveness probe at a dependency.

title: Expose payments-api inside the cluster
author: Kofi Mensah
description: The ledger worker needs to call payments-api directly instead of going out through the public ingress. Adds a ClusterIP Service on port 80 in front of the existing Deployment.

explanation.cause: The Service selects app: payment-api, but the pods are labelled app: payments-api, so it matches nothing.
explanation.why: A Service with no matching pods has no endpoints: the ledger worker would get connection refused on every call. The selector has to match the pod template labels exactly.

title: Snapshot pruning deleted this week and kept last spring
ticket: We went to restore orders-db from a snapshot and the newest one was 15 days old. The nightly prune job runs with RETAIN_DAYS=14, and its log shows it deleting snapshots taken the day before.

lines: def prune_snapshots(client, volume_id: str, retain_days: int, now: datetime) -> list[str]:

explanation.cause: cutoff is the oldest moment worth keeping, so anything created after it is inside the retention window. The comparison deleted those and kept the old ones.
explanation.why: The job quietly removed every recent restore point while hoarding stale ones. Snapshots older than the cutoff are the ones to delete; flipping to >= or nudging the cutoff by a day still deletes the newest.

title: Retries hit ledger-db in waves after every failover
ticket: ledger-db failed over for 20 seconds and then fell over twice more. Its connection graph shows spikes of 40k requests at exactly 100ms, 200ms, 400ms and 800ms after each failure, one per retry, from every API pod at once.

lines: // Backoff is how long a client waits before retry attempt n, counting from 0.

output: backoff_test.go:28: 1000 calls to Backoff(3) returned 1 distinct value (800ms)

explanation.cause: The backoff grows and is capped, but it has no jitter: every client that failed at the same moment retries at the same moment.
explanation.why: Synchronized retries arrive as one spike per attempt and knock the recovering database over again. Full jitter picks a random delay up to the backoff; ten nanoseconds of noise is still lockstep, a delay under baseDelay drops the growth, and doubling just makes two spikes.

title: Give the backup job its own IAM policy
author: Ana Ruiz
description: Moves db-backup off the shared ops role. It writes nightly dumps and prunes anything past 30 days. ListBucket can't be limited to a key prefix through the Resource field anyway, so the prune statement uses a wildcard to keep it simple.

explanation.cause: arn:aws:s3:::* matches every bucket and every object in the account, and the same statement grants s3:DeleteObject.
explanation.why: A bug or a leaked credential in the backup job could now delete any object anywhere, including the backups it exists to protect. Scope the statement to the backups bucket ARN for ListBucket and orders-db-backups/nightly/* for DeleteObject.

title: Page on error budget burn instead of raw 5xx count
author: Jonas Weber
description: The old alert paged at 5 errors a second whatever the traffic, so it fired every Saturday peak and slept through quiet-hour outages. This pages when checkout-api burns its 99.9% budget 14.4x too fast over both the last hour and the last 5 minutes. Slow-burn ticket alert follows.

explanation.cause: Nothing wrong: both windows divide errors by total requests for the same service, and 14.4 x 0.001 is the standard fast-burn threshold for a 99.9% SLO.
explanation.why: The long window proves the burn is real, the short one stops the page lingering after recovery, and the and matches because both sides aggregate by service. At 14.4x, 2% of a 30-day budget is gone in an hour, which is worth waking someone.
